anchors: The start script picks its config by name: `host#<md5 of the hostname>.json`
This is for the same machine under a new name only.
decision: A host whose unit exits 1 at start after a hostname change is confirmed by comparing md5 of the hostname with the one host#*.json name, and repaired by backing up and renaming host#<old hash>.* to the new hash and restarting the unit, with no re-registration and no OAuth code. A copy of another host given a new hostname is excluded and follows the cloned-host section.

evidence.text: Read from the installed chrome-remote-desktop 151.0.7922.13 start script: g_host_hash = md5(socket.gethostname()); config_file = host#<hash>.json; a missing file prints 'Failed to load config: ...' and returns 1. printf %s "$(hostname)" | md5sum equals that hash on the test box. The shipped bash block ran against scratch config dirs: renamed (moved .json and .display_layout.pb, backup made), none, already matching and two files (each refused, rc 1). Inherited from the queued report: on a renamed host running 142.0.7444.18 the unit exited with no error line and, after the move, logged 'Host ready to receive connections' with no re-registration. RED: haiku on the old text found no cause; opus answered NONE from the text.

reopen_if: A CRD release stops keying the config file name on the hostname, or a moved config is shown to need re-registration.
why: The start script picks its config as host#<md5(socket.gethostname())>.json, so after a rename it finds no config and exits 1, possibly with no clear error line. The registration (host_id, private_key) is intact, so re-registering spends a single-use code for nothing; the old text pointed only at the generic offline row and the re-registration path. On a clone the same move would bring the copy up as the source.

anchors: use the user bus whenever its socket exists, and start a private bus only as the fallback
decision: A browser that takes about 25 s to start inside a CRD session is checked for a session file that starts its own bus with dbus-launch: confirm by reading the desktop's DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS and timing an org.freedesktop.secrets Peer.Ping on that bus and on /run/user/<uid>/bus as the control, and fix the session file to use the user bus when its socket exists, with dbus-launch only as the fallback. Starting a keyring daemon in the session file is named as the wrong fix.

evidence.text: On a host running chrome-remote-desktop 151.0.7922.13 with a dbus-launch session file, the desktop's bus was a /tmp/dbus-... address while the CRD unit's own environment held unix:path=/run/user/<uid>/bus; the skill's confirm block run as root gave NoReply after 25.03 s on the desktop bus and 0.007 s on the user bus. The launcher source copies its full environment into the session (_init_child_env) and starts the file via /bin/sh. The fix block was executed under dash with stubbed tools on both branches. RED probes (opus, haiku) on the pre-edit text found no covering line; GREEN probes are in the checklist.

reopen_if: The launcher stops forwarding its environment to the session file, the keyring becomes reachable from a dbus-launch bus, or a measured private-bus Ping answers fast on a current release.
why: A private session bus cannot reach the keyring that runs on the systemd user bus, so every Secret Service call waits out the 25 s libdbus reply timeout while CPU, memory and the browser look healthy; the skill was silent on the session bus and readers chased CPU, DNS and portal causes or started a keyring on the wrong bus.
